title: Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain.
PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1.
METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care (PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, satisfaction, adverse events, and costs.
RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) (Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was maintained.
CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.

title: Non-Surgical Therapies for Knee Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence and Emerging Strategies.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by pain, stiffness, and functional impairment. As many patients seek to avoid surgery, a synthesis of conservative treatment options is clinically relevant for evidence-based management.
METHODS: A structured PubMed literature search was conducted through December 15, 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, cohort and case-control studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses evaluating nonsurgical interventions for knee OA. Extracted outcomes included pain, function, safety, and comparative effectiveness across reported follow-up durations.
RESULTS: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (HA) has a favorable safety profile and may delay progression to total knee arthroplasty, though benefits over placebo are modest and guideline recommendations inconsistent. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) improves pain and function and may outperform HA, although outcomes vary with preparation methods and study quality. Autologous conditioned serum and dextrose prolotherapy demonstrate symptomatic benefit, whereas corticosteroid injections primarily provide short-term relief. Disease-modifying osteoarthritis drugs (DMOADs), including sprifermin, lorecivivint, LNA043, cathepsin-K inhibition, ADAMTS-5 inhibition, and repurposed metabolic agents such as metformin, are emerging investigational strategies with variable structural and symptomatic results. Early evidence suggests mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies may improve outcomes but remain investigational. Core conservative measures, including exercise therapy, physical therapy, and weight reduction, consistently reduce pain and improve function. Assistive devices and valgus bracing provide additional symptomatic and biomechanical benefit. Among device-based interventions, cooled radiofrequency ablation offers durable pain relief compared with HA or corticosteroids, while sustained acoustic medicine and extracorporeal shockwave therapy show functional improvement; evidence for pulsed electromagnetic field therapy is mixed. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provide effective analgesia with reduced systemic risk.
CONCLUSION: Non-surgical management of knee OA should follow a stepwise approach, with rehabilitation and weight optimization as first-line therapy, selective injection- and device-based options for persistent symptoms, and timely surgical referral when disability remains refractory. Future progress will depend on standardized protocols and higher-quality long-term comparative trials to improve treatment selection and disease modification.

title: Management of Hand Injuries: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Surgical and Rehabilitation Strategies.
abstract: Management of traumatic hand injuries has evolved substantially with advances in anesthesia, tendon repair, biological adjuncts, fracture fixation, and rehabilitation. This systematic review synthesizes contemporary evidence on surgical and rehabilitation strategies for improving functional recovery and reducing complications after acute hand trauma. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261320700). PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for studies published from January 2000 to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials and prospective comparative studies evaluating contemporary strategies for flexor or extensor tendon injuries and metacarpal or phalangeal fractures were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Of 3417 records identified, 354 duplicates were removed and 3063 records were screened. Following full-text assessment, 23 studies were included. Evidence supported the use of wide-awake local anesthesia no tourniquet (WALANT) as a safe alternative to general anesthesia, although functional superiority was not consistent across trials. Acellular dermal matrices, biological amnion, hydrogels, hyaluronic acid, and other adjuncts showed potential for reducing adhesions and improving tendon gliding. Early active mobilization and place-and-hold protocols produced favorable functional outcomes, while relative motion extension orthoses improved early function after extensor tendon repair. Smartphone-assisted rehabilitation improved adherence. Headless compression screws facilitated earlier functional recovery in selected metacarpal fractures, while multistrand tendon repairs provided sufficient strength for early mobilization. Contemporary hand injury management increasingly integrates WALANT, robust tendon repair, anti-adhesion adjuncts, early active rehabilitation, modern orthoses, and digital adherence tools. However, heterogeneity and variable risk of bias across studies warrant cautious interpretation and further high-quality comparative research.

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss.
METHODS: Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).
RESULTS: (1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min.
CONCLUSION: Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.

title: Analgesic efficacy of regional and local analgesic techniques for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in adults undergoing general anesthesia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute pain after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) can impair early mobility and rehabilitation. This network meta-analysis (NMA) compared regional and local analgesic techniques in adults undergoing ACLR under general anesthesia.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to February 18, 2026, for randomized controlled trials. Risk of bias was assessed utilizing the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB2), and a Bayesian random-effects NMA was performed.
RESULTS: Thirty-one studies involving 2,470 patients were included. Only six were at low risk of bias. For oral morphine milligram equivalents (OMME) at 24 h postoperatively, femoral nerve block (FNB) [mean difference (MD) = - 30.31, 95% credible interval (CrI) - 58.02, - 6.79] and FNB with sciatic nerve block (SNB) [MD = - 40.42, 95% CrI - 80.42, - 5.79] were associated with lower estimated opioid consumption than control. FNB with SNB ranked highest for lower 24-h OMME [surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) = 87.44%]. FNB with graft donor-site infiltration was associated with lower estimated pain scores in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) than local infiltration analgesia (MD = - 2.46, 95% CrI: -4.67, - 0.21). At 24 h, adductor canal block (ACB) with graft donor-site infiltration had lower estimated pain scores than ACB (MD = - 1.50, 95% CrI: -2.43, - 0.61). At 48 h, the 95% CrIs for all pain comparisons included 0. ACB with infiltration between the popliteal artery and capsule of the posterior knee (iPACK) had a longer estimated time to first analgesic request (TFAR) than ACB (MD = 7.50, 95% CrI: 1.92, 13.01). Regarding postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), the 95% CrIs for all comparisons included 1. In sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk studies, the CrIs for key comparisons regarding OMME and TFAR widened and included 0. Some treatment nodes were missing from certain outcome networks, and the rankings for PONV changed.
CONCLUSION: Potential analgesic benefits varied across outcomes, but key estimates became less precise after high-risk studies were excluded. Functional outcomes were not systematically synthesized, and adverse event assessment was limited to PONV. These findings do not establish the overall clinical superiority of any single strategy.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 and 12 months between these treatment groups.
METHODS: Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time points in both groups.
RESULTS: A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm3 ± 6.8, p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus (AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% (13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial.

title: Female Team-Sport Athletes' Physical Fitness and Jump Performance Kinematics After Plyometric Jump Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plyometric jump training (PJT) can improve athletes' physical fitness across a range of sports and populations. Nonetheless, the role of PJT in adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics remains unclear, particularly given the increasing number of published, heterogeneous studies.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to first examine the effectiveness of PJT in improving physical fitness and jump-performance kinematics in adult female team-sport athletes, and second, to provide evidence-based recommendations for PJT prescription for this population.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO databases up to March 2026. The included studies recruited healthy female team-sport athletes (mean age: ≥ 18 years), incorporated a PJT programme ≥ 2 weeks in duration, included comparator groups, and assessed athletes' physical fitness, jump performance, and/or kinematics. The risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Hedges' g effect sizes (ES) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) were reported using a random-effects model for meta-analyses. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the participant characteristics (height, body mass, sport) and PJT programming variables (duration, frequency, total sessions, weekly total jumps). The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Thirty-one articles were included (n = 609 participants), and 25 were meta-analysed. Two studies were categorised with high RoB (≤ 3 points), 20 studies achieved moderate RoB (4-5 points), and 9 studies achieved low RoB (≥ 6 points). Compared to controls, PJT improved countermovement jump (CMJ) height (ES = 0.550, p < 0.001), CMJ peak concentric velocity (ES = 0.623, p = 0.011), drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) (ES = 0.926, p = 0.001), DJ height (ES = 0.721, p = 0.002), 10 m sprint time (ES = 0.712, p = 0.032), 20 m sprint time (ES = 0.709, p < 0.001), 30 m sprint time (ES = 1.018, p = 0.001), non-linear (agility) Illinois test time (ES = 1.225, p < 0.001) and T test sprint time (ES = 0.965, p < 0.001). Compared to PJT ≤ 6 weeks, longer interventions favoured DJ RSI (p = 0.008), 10 m sprint time (p = 0.001), and Illinois agility test time (p < 0.001). Impact of heterogeneity (I2) remained low (≤ 0.06%) in five analyses and moderate in the other four analyses (≤ 73.1%). The certainty of evidence was considered low to moderate for the study outcomes. Two studies reported that a total of three participants possibly sustained an injury during PJT.
CONCLUSIONS: Adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics improved after PJT when compared to the control condition, including CMJ height, CMJ peak concentric velocity, DJ RSI, linear sprint speed, and non-linear (agility) sprint speed. The improvements were particularly notable with longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks).

title: Conservative and Post-Operative Rehabilitation Protocols for Hip Dysplasia in Adolescents to Adulthood: A Literature Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is a spectrum of structural abnormalities associated with insufficient acetabular coverage, predisposing adults to labral pathology, chondral wear, and early-onset osteoarthritis. Despite a range of conservative and post-operative management options, key aspects of physiotherapy rehabilitation remain poorly defined, including intervention timing, progressive loading criteria and exercise selection in those with DDH. The purpose of this review is to examine conservative and post-operative rehabilitation protocols and associated functional outcomes in adolescents and adults aged 13-50 years with DDH.
METHODS: A structured electronic search of MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science Core Collection was used to identify English-language, peer-reviewed literature addressing physiotherapy rehabilitation for DDH. Twelve sources met inclusion criteria, comprising randomized controlled trials, Delphi consensus studies, a retrospective case series, and observational designs. Data were extracted regarding intervention type, progression criteria, patient-reported outcome measures, and return to sport measures.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Twelve sources were included, comprising adolescent and adult cohorts aged 13-50 years, with one source exclusively including an adolescent population aged 5-17 years.1 Conservative rehabilitation commonly emphasised hip abductor, extensor and hip external rotator strengthening combined with lumbopelvic stability and movement pattern retraining. Post-operative protocols applied phased, criterion-based progressions guided by pain-free range of motion, ≥80% hip abductor strength symmetry, and functional stability testing. The overall evidence base was limited by methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, reliance on expert consensus, with no high-quality comparative trials identified.
CONCLUSION: Current evidence tentatively supports physiotherapy as a central component of both conservative and post-operative rehabilitation for adolescents and adults with DDH, with multimodal, criterion-based approaches incorporating progressive strengthening and neuromuscular retraining most consistently described across included sources. Standardized rehabilitation frameworks and validated progression criteria are needed to optimize functional outcomes in this population.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 5.

title: Return-to-Play Outcomes After Primary Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Vary Substantially Depending on Return Criteria: A Systematic Review Stratified by Competition Level.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine how return definitions influence return to play (RTP), return to the same level of play (RTSP), advancement rates, and return timelines after primary ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (UCLR) in baseball pitchers across levels of competition.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched from January 2000 to January 2025. Studies evaluating baseball pitchers undergoing primary UCLR and reporting RTP, RTSP, advancement, or return timing outcomes with participation-based (RTP based on a single event) or durability-based (RTP after sustained participation over a predefined threshold) criteria were included. Primary outcomes were RTP, RTSP, and advancement rate (progression to a higher level after UCLR); secondary outcome was return time stratified by return criteria. Risk of bias was assessed with the Methodological Index for Non-randomized Studies and Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tools.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies met inclusion. Across these studies, 19 included Major League Baseball players (2194 players), 5 included Minor League Baseball (MiLB) players (2318 players), 4 included collegiate athletes (553 athletes), and 6 included high school athletes (258 athletes). RTP/RTSP rates were 86% to 92%/70% to 87% in high school, 84%/67% to 92% in college, 76.3% to 79%/69.1% to 100% in MiLB, and 80% to 97.2%/28.1% to 87% in Major League Baseball. Advancement was 55.7% to 63.2% in high school, 4.1% to 44.4% in college, and 22.3% to 45% in MiLB. Surgery-to-return time using the common RTSP definition ranged from 13.7 to 20.5 months (Major League Baseball), 14.6 to 16.4 (MiLB), and 11 to 17 (college and high school). Durability-based definitions were not consistently associated with longer return intervals.
CONCLUSIONS: Without standardized return criteria, reported RTP, RTSP, advancement rates, and return timelines after primary UCLR in baseball pitchers varied substantially across studies and competition levels. Durability-based criteria were not consistently associated with longer return timelines, indicating that return outcomes should be interpreted according to the competition level and return definition used. Standardized, tier-specific return criteria may improve clinical interpretation after primary UCLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV studies.

title: Fueling the Modern Endurance Athlete: The High-Carbohydrate Revolution, Exogenous Ketones, and an Evidence-Based Approach for the Sports Medicine Clinician.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Carbohydrate is the principal limiting fuel for prolonged, high-intensity endurance exercise, and consensus guidelines have long capped recommended intake during exercise at approximately 90 g/h. Two developments have challenged and extended contemporary fueling practice: a shift toward carbohydrate intakes of 100 to 150 g/h in elite endurance sport, and widespread commercial availability of exogenous ketone supplements marketed as ergogenic aids. Both have outpaced the clinical evidence and have reached the competitive and recreational athletes who present to sports medicine clinicians.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Narrative review of primary metabolic and performance studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus statements published through mid-2026, identified through PubMed and reference tracing.
STUDY DESIGN: Narrative review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 5.
RESULTS: Multiple-transportable-carbohydrate formulations (glucose plus fructose) raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation above the roughly 1 g/minute ceiling imposed by intestinal glucose transport, providing the mechanistic basis for fueling rates of ≥90 g/h. Ingesting 120 g/h increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, but the best-controlled studies have not demonstrated additional endogenous (liver and muscle) glycogen sparing or a consistent performance advantage, and gastrointestinal tolerability requires deliberate gut training. For exogenous ketones, an influential 2016 study reported altered substrate use and improved time-trial performance. Subsequent trials and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have not confirmed an acute ergogenic effect, and several have documented gastrointestinal distress or impaired performance. The more promising and reproducible signal for ketones lies in postexercise recovery and attenuation of overreaching. Finally, athletes who restrict in-competition and training carbohydrate to pursue leanness risk low energy and carbohydrate availability, the substrate of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).
CONCLUSION: Carbohydrate intake of ≤90 g/h, built through progressive gut training, is supported by consensus guidelines and mechanistic evidence for prolonged, high-intensity endurance events; progression toward 120 g/h is reasonable in selected, well-adapted athletes competing in the longest events, with the understanding that a performance benefit >90 g/h remains unproven. Routine exogenous ketone supplementation for acute performance is not supported by current evidence; a recovery-focused application is plausible and increasingly supported but requires further study. Clinicians should frame both strategies within adequate energy availability to protect long-term athlete health.Strength-of-Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT):B.

title: Long Head of Biceps Tenodesis: Fixation Constructs and Tenodesis Level-A Narrative Review.
abstract: Disorders of the long head of the biceps tendon (LHBT) are a common source of anterior shoulder pain and are frequently encountered in patients undergoing shoulder surgery. Biceps tenodesis has gained popularity because it addresses biceps-related symptoms while preserving muscle contour and function. This narrative review summarizes contemporary evidence on LHBT tenodesis, with particular emphasis on fixation constructs and tenodesis level, and integrates current evidence into a practical framework for surgical decision-making. A literature review was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar, incorporating clinical studies, biomechanical investigations, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses evaluating tenodesis techniques, fixation methods, outcomes, and complications. Current evidence indicates that top-of-groove, suprapectoral, and subpectoral tenodesis can provide favorable pain and functional outcomes, with comparative clinical studies generally demonstrating limited clinically meaningful differences between levels. Subpectoral tenodesis may more completely address groove-related pathology but is associated with approach-specific risks, whereas biomechanical differences among interference screws, suture anchors, cortical buttons, and onlay constructs have not consistently translated into differences in clinical outcomes. Rehabilitation protocols vary considerably and are commonly influenced by concomitant procedures. The available evidence is limited by heterogeneous techniques and patient populations, relatively few randomized comparisons, and limited long-term follow-up. Accordingly, no single tenodesis level or fixation construct can currently be considered universally superior. Patient-specific factors, groove pathology, surgical context, and the strength and applicability of the available evidence should inform individualized surgical decision-making.

title: The longitudinal relationship between physical capacity and self-perceived physical functioning after total hip and knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine longitudinal within-person effects between capacity and self-perceived performance during postoperative physiotherapy in patients with total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA/TKA).
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of a cluster randomized controlled trial on physiotherapy after THA and TKA using random intercept cross lagged panel models. Capacity was assessed with the 40-m fast-paced walk test (40 m FPWT) and the 30-s chair-stand test (30-s CST), and self-perceived performance with the Oxford Hip/Knee Score functioning subscale (OHS/OKS) and the Hip disability/Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical function Short form (HOOS-PS/KOOS-PS). Assessments were performed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months postoperatively.
RESULTS: 312 THA (mean age 66, SD: 9; 53% female) and 312 TKA (mean age 67, SD: 8; 55% female) were included. From pre-surgery to 3 months, no effects were found between capacity and self-perceived performance in either THA or TKA.From 3 to 12 months, in THA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect (β 0.34, 95% CI 0.05-0.63) on HOOS-PS scores at 12 months. In TKA, 40 m FPWT performance at 3 months had a positive effect on both OKS functioning (β 0.24 95% CI 0.05-0.43) and KOOS-PS (β 0.29 95% CI 0.11-0.47) scores at 12 months. No other effects were observed.
CONCLUSION: From pre-surgery to 3 months, capacity and self-perceived performance showed no effects within individuals. However, during the early postoperative phase, gait speed may be a relevant treatment target to improve long-term self-perceived performance.

title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting.
METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed.
RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

title: Effects of Oral L-Arginine on Everyday Persistent Fatigue, Sleep, and Post-Exercise Lactate Recovery in Community-Dwelling Working-Age Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The evidence for nutritional interventions against fatigue is limited; we evaluated whether L-arginine reduces fatigue in working-age adults.
METHODS: In this 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 community-dwelling working-age adults aged 30-59 years with persistent fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] total ≥ 27) received oral L-arginine 3 g/day, 6 g/day, or placebo. The primary endpoint was FSS change; secondary endpoints included the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and blood lactate kinetics during a standardized submaximal treadmill run (~70% VO2max, 30 min). Data from 119 participants were analyzed, with Holm adjustment for multiplicity.
RESULTS: At Week 8, FSS decreased more with 6 g/day than with placebo (-6.41 vs. -2.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.024), whereas 3 g/day did not differ from placebo. The 6 g/day CIS improvement did not survive multiplicity adjustment. PSQI scores improved nominally at both doses (3 g/day, p = 0.007; 6 g/day, p = 0.045). With 6 g/day, the total lactate area under the curve (Holm-adjusted p = 0.041) and 15-min recovery lactate (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002) were lower than with the placebo, whereas the resting plasma nitrite did not differ. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: L-arginine supplementation at 6 g/day for 8 weeks reduced fatigue severity relative to placebo and was well-tolerated; however, mean FSS scores remained above the enrollment threshold, indicating a reduction in, rather than resolution of, persistent fatigue.

title: Effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate on exercise-induced biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation in federated road cyclists.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of a chickpea protein hydrolysate (CPH) on biomarkers associated with exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation in federated male road cyclists.
METHODS: Twenty-four participants completed a 14-day intervention receiving either 12 g/day of chickpea protein hydrolysate (EXP) or a placebo (PLA) following training sessions. The selected dose was based on previous studies demonstrating antioxidant and immunomodulatory bioactive properties of the hydrolysate. Nutritional intake and training were registered. Body composition and biochemical markers of muscle damage and inflammation were assessed before and after the study.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in body composition, training load, or dietary intake between groups, indicating controlled experimental conditions. However, between-group analyses of change scores revealed significant differences for lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; p = 0.04) and C-reactive protein (CRP; p = 0.02), favoring the experimental group. LDH decreased in the EXP group while increasing slightly in the placebo group, whereas CRP decreased in EXP and increased in PLA. Although creatine kinase (CK) showed a favorable pattern in the EXP group, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). Myoglobin followed a similar downward trend. The high baseline protein intake (>2 g/kg/day) and short intervention duration may have limited changes in body composition, nevertheless, the observed biomarker responses suggest that CPH supplementation may influence selected physiological processes associated with exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress.
CONCLUSIONS: In trained cyclists with high habitual protein intakes, 14 days of CPH supplementation did not alter body composition but was associated with favorable changes in selected biomarkers related to exercise-induced inflammation and cellular stress compared with placebo. Given the short intervention period and the absence of direct assessments of recovery or performance, these findings should be interpreted as short-term biochemical responses. Further studies are required to determine their physiological relevance and whether these biomarker changes translate into meaningful improvements in recovery, training adaptation, or athletic performance.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.

title: Effects of Exercise Type and Duration on Pain, Function, and Quality of Life in Patients With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review With Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the effects of aerobic exercise, resistance exercise, and combined interventions on pain, function, and quality of life (QoL) in patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA) at the short term (≤12 weeks) and long term (>12 weeks). DESIGN: Intervention systematic review with Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA). LITERATURE SEARCH: MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE, CENTRAL, CINAHL, PEDro, AMED, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception until July 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomized controlled trials of patients with knee OA that evaluated exercise interventions aimed at improving pain, function, and QoL. DATA SYNTHESIS: Using random-effects models, the NMA synthesized effect sizes and ranked interventions by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), with evidence certainty assessed via the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. RESULTS: Thirty-five trials (n = 3808 patients) were included. For pain, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect among the interventions (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.937, low certainty). For function, short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect estimates (SMD = -0.590, low certainty), followed by long-term aerobic exercise (SMD = -0.540, very low certainty). Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effect (SMD = 0.663, low certainty) for improving QoL. CONCLUSION: Aerobic and resistance exercise, alone or in combination, and delivered over the short- or long-term, improved pain, function, and QoL for patients with knee OA. Short-term combined aerobic and resistance exercise had clinically meaningful improvements for pain, with relatively favorable effects on function and QoL. Evidence regarding the clinical significance of long-term exercise interventions was limited. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(11):724-734. Epub 24 July 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.13875.

title: First-Hand Experience and the Value of Telerehabilitation for Chronic Knee Pain: A Discrete Choice Experiment Nested in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess whether first-hand experience of receiving physical therapy via telerehabilitation affected patient preferences and willingness to pay for telerehabilitation. DESIGN: This study used a discrete choice experiment nested within a randomized controlled trial. METHODS: We recruited 319 Australian adults aged 45 years or over, with chronic knee pain consistent with osteoarthritis, who had completed a clinical trial where they were randomized to receive physical therapy via telerehabilitation or in-person. Participants were presented hypothetical scenarios and asked to choose between physical therapy delivered via telerehabilitation or in-person. Each scenario presented seven attributes of consultations at varying levels. Data were analyzed using a generalized multinomial logit and latent class models. RESULTS: There were 164 participants from the in-person trial arm (80% of those randomized) and 155 from the telerehabilitation arm (82% of those randomized) who participated. Participants in the telerehabilitation arm (ie, with first-hand experience of telerehabilitation) were willing to pay AU$ 87.49 (95% confidence interval: 72.83, 102.14) more than people in the in-person arm for telerehabilitation consultations (all other attributes fixed at reference values for categorical variables and at mean values for continuous variables). Four subgroups were identified. In the telerehabilitation arm, 105 (68% of 155) participants preferred telerehabilitation, and 50 (32%) preferred in-person consultations. In the in-person arm, 63 (39% of 164) held a strong preference for in-person consultations, and 101 (61%) had a mild preference for in-person consultations. CONCLUSION: People with first-hand experience using telerehabilitation for physical therapy expressed a greater willingness to use and pay for it than people who experienced in-person care. title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.

title: The Effect of a Bioactive Fabric Sleeve on Flexor-Pronator Recovery in Collegiate Baseball Pitchers: A Pilot Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fatigue of the flexor-pronator mass could lead to increased stresses on the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) and potential injury. Soreness is a clinical indicator of fatigue. If flexor-pronator soreness recovery could be improved, there is potential protection of the UCL in baseball throwers. Hypothesis/Purpose The purpose of this study was to investigate the efficacy of a bioactive fabric sleeve in enhancing subjective recovery in high-level pitchers who experience soft tissue soreness around the elbow. The investigators hypothesized that the use of the bioactive fabric, non-compressive sleeve would lead to a significant reduction in subjective elbow soreness the day following in-game pitching competition.
STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort pilot study.
METHODS: Health Division I collegiate baseball pitchers were recruited to participate. The intervention consisted of two sleeve types: a control standard elbow compression sleeve and the experimental bioactive fabric, non-compressive sleeve, worn the night after their pitching performance to bed and removed the following morning. The main outcome measure was subjective reported soreness in the soft tissues of the medial elbow reported the night of and the day after the pitching appearance in a collegiate baseball game. The length of the study encompassed the duration of the spring baseball season, allowing for multiple evaluations throughout the pitchers' regular game schedules. A multivariable mixed-effects linear regression model was used to analyze changes in subjective pain and soreness between the bioactive, non-compressive, fabric sleeve and control sleeves, adjusting for time of season and accounting for multiple data points per pitcher.
RESULTS: The bioactive fabric, non-compressive sleeve resulted in a statistically significant reduction in subjective reporting of pain the morning after pitching compared with reported pain the night of pitching (p=0.044) versus the change associated with a control sleeve.
CONCLUSION: This study showed the bioactive fabric was safe and demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in subjective reporting of medial elbow pain. Successful implementation of the study design was accomplished with high-level baseball pitchers. Future studies should involve a greater number of athletes with more granular assessment considering actual pitching workload.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II.

title: From Signal to Biological Meaning: A Systematic Review of Construct-Validity Evidence for External Training Load Metrics in Sport.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: External training load (ETL) metrics describe external work but often imply metabolic demand, neuromuscular load, tissue stress, fatigue, or adaptation. These interpretations require construct-validity evidence beyond device accuracy or reliability.
METHODS: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Academic Search Ultimate from inception to March 2026; final searches were on 1 March, except Embase on 7 March. Eligible peer-reviewed English studies evaluated an ETL indicator and its interpreted construct in athletes or physically active participants. Reports limited to technical accuracy, reliability, measurement error, or descriptive monitoring were excluded. We adjudicated one page-anchored construct-evidence chain per study. Measurement-property analyses used review-adapted COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments (COSMIN); prediction models used the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool plus Artificial Intelligence (PROBAST+AI); other designs used Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tools. Conceptual and methodological heterogeneity across metrics, target constructs, comparators, and study designs precluded meaningful meta-analysis; therefore, we used evidence maps and narrative synthesis.
RESULTS: Forty-six studies contributed 46 primary evidence chains. Main study samples ranged from 7 to 71 participants, with smaller analysis-specific subsamples; most studies included only men. Construct attribution was explicit in 14 studies and explicit but qualified in 26; four were implicit but qualified and two reverse-target. Thirteen studies (28%) used a direct construct-matched criterion. Alternative proxies supported 16 studies (35%), condition or group contrasts 11 (24%), and mixed routes six (13%). General exercise intensity was the most frequent construct family (15 studies, 33%). Appraisal identified common limitations in hypotheses testing and analysis. Nineteen studies (41%) explicitly distinguished technical performance from construct interpretation, and 12 (26%) explicitly justified comparator selection.
CONCLUSIONS: Most ETL metrics were supported as descriptions of external movement, work, or exposure rather than direct indicators of biological demand or response. Biological interpretations require an explicit construct, plausible mechanism, directional hypothesis, and construct-matched reference. Heterogeneity and methodological limitations reduce confidence in biological interpretations.

title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

title: Biomaterial-assisted culture of mesenchymal stem cells for enhanced extracellular vesicle production and cartilage regeneration: a systematic review.
abstract: Articular cartilage has limited self-repair capacity, prompting interest in cell-free therapies such as extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). This systematic review assessed whether MSCs cultured with biomaterials produce more EVs, and EVs with greater chondrogenic or cartilage-regenerative efficacy, than MSCs in conventional culture. The publications were searched on PubMed, Scopus, and EBSCO (2016-2026), and the synthesis of the evidence was done narratively, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. From 576 unique records, we included 14 preclinical studies: 12 used biomaterials in a three-dimensional format, and two cultured MSCs on decellularized extracellular matrix. Eleven compared biomaterial-culture EVs head-to-head with conventional-culture EVs for chondrogenic or cartilage-repair outcomes. EV yield was higher with the biomaterial in all ten studies that compared it (about 1.2- to 7.5-fold per cell or per unit of protein). In all 11 comparisons, biomaterial-culture EVs matched or exceeded conventional-culture EVs in chondrocyte proliferation, chondrogenic marker expression, matrix deposition, or in vivo cartilage repair. Cargo-target mechanisms were functionally validated in six studies, although in one the microRNA had been enriched by transfection rather than by the culture platform. Certainty of evidence was low for yield and very low for chondrogenic, cartilage-repair, and anti-inflammatory outcomes. Risk of bias was probably low in seven studies and probably high in seven. The comparator arms often differed in more than the biomaterial, and EV characterization was frequently incomplete. In conclusion, biomaterial-assisted culture is a promising but not yet standardized route to more chondrogenic MSC-derived EVs and requires further study.

title: AAOS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Synopsis and Practice Implications.
abstract:
DESCRIPTION: Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common peripheral nerve compression frequently encountered in primary care and internal medicine settings. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) developed updated evidence-based clinical practice guidelines in 2024 to improve outcomes and optimize diagnosis and management. This synopsis highlights recommendations most relevant to nonoperative clinicians, with an emphasis on efficient diagnosis, management, and appropriate referral.
METHODS: The AAOS guideline was developed by a multidisciplinary panel using a systematic review of the available literature. Guideline development involved reviewing the evidence, formulating recommendations, and grading them based on the strength of evidence and consensus, in line with established standards for trustworthy clinical practice guidelines.
RECOMMENDATIONS: The guidelines emphasize that carpal tunnel syndrome is a clinical diagnosis based on characteristic symptoms and examination findings. Strong evidence supports the use of validated clinical tools, such as the Carpal Tunnel Syndrome-6 (CTS-6), in patients with typical presentations, without routine reliance on ultrasonography or electrodiagnostic testing, which may be reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or potentially recurrent cases. Nonoperative therapies may provide short-term symptom relief; for example, corticosteroid injection demonstrates short-term benefit but does not alter the long-term disease course. Many commonly used interventions, including therapeutic ultrasound, oral corticosteroids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and platelet-rich plasma injections, lack evidence of clinical benefit and thus are not recommended. Surgical carpal tunnel release, when pursued for moderate to severe symptoms, thenar atrophy, or failure of nonoperative management, may be performed via open or endoscopic release. The guidelines recommend against routine pre-operative testing in otherwise healthy patients. These recommendations support efficient diagnosis, appropriate management, and timely referral while reducing unnecessary testing and low-value care.

title: Dosage and safety of non-invasive brain stimulation for chronic musculoskeletal pain management: a scoping review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To map stimulation targets and dosage parameters used in non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS), including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), theta-burst stimulation (TBS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) for chronic musculoskeletal pain (CMP), and to synthesise rationale for dosage selection, safety monitoring and adverse event reporting.
DESIGN: The scoping review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, using the Arksey and O'Malley framework.
DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE (PubMed), Scopus, Web of Science and Embase were searched from their inception to 16 October 2025.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Studies involving adults with CMP receiving rTMS, TBS or tDCS were eligible if they reported at least one of the following outcomes: stimulation targets, dosage parameters or safety. All study designs were eligible.
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data. Findings were synthesised descriptively by modality, target, dosage characteristics, rationale for parameter selection and safety monitoring.
RESULTS: A total of 123 studies were included, predominantly randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving fibromyalgia, knee osteoarthritis and chronic low back pain. The primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were the most frequently targeted regions for stimulation. Common protocols used 10 Hz rTMS at 80–120% rest motor threshold and tDCS at 1–2 mA for 20–30 min. Treatment schedule varied substantially, ranging from 1 to 60 sessions, and most delivered at five sessions per week over 2 to 4 weeks. Stimulation targets were justified in 63% of studies, whereas rationales for frequency, intensity and number of sessions were reported inconsistently. The method used for adverse events monitoring was not clearly described in 62% of studies. Among the 113 studies in which participants actually received NIBS, reported adverse events were predominantly mild and transient. However, adverse event ascertainment and reporting were inconsistent and the reported percentages represented the proportion of studies reporting each adverse event rather than participant-level incidence. Therefore, these data do not permit reliable estimation of adverse event frequency.
CONCLUSION: Current NIBS dosage for management of CMP remains heterogeneous and driven by empirical experience. Safety reporting is inadequate. Although reported adverse events were predominantly mild and transient, inconsistent adverse event ascertainment and reporting preclude reliable conclusion about the safety profile of NIBS. Greater emphasis on brain network theory-informed targets in people with CMP, systematic and personalised dosage optimisation, and standardised safety reporting is needed to support evidence-based clinical implementation.

title: Meniscal Repair Achieves Comparable Mid-Term Functional Performance to Partial Meniscectomy Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction in Highly Active Patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Concomitant meniscal injuries accompany 40%-60% of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures. Surgeons often face a clinical choice between meniscal repair, which prioritizes long-term joint preservation, and partial meniscectomy, which is traditionally perceived to facilitate earlier functional recovery. Despite the biological advantages of repair, persistent concerns remain that its restrictive postoperative protocols might impede mid-term functional performance compared to meniscectomy. This study aims to compare quadriceps/hamstring strength, dynamic balance, functional hop performance, and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) at 2-5 years post-ACLR between patients undergoing concomitant meniscal repair versus partial meniscectomy.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study evaluated highly active patients who underwent ACLR between 2019 and 2023. Of 68 patients who underwent ACLR with a concomitant meniscal injury and a pre-injury Tegner score ≥ 6,16 were excluded: 5 due to revision ACLR or secondary meniscal procedures during the follow-up period, 8 due to concurrent multi-ligament injuries or full-thickness articular cartilage defects requiring surgery, and 3 due to knee joint deformities (varus or valgus malalignment > 5°)The remaining 52 patients were stratified into meniscal repair (n = 20) or partial meniscectomy (n = 32) groups. Outcomes included isokinetic strength (60°/s, 180°/s; Limb Symmetry Index, LSI), Y-balance test, single-leg hop (SLH), and PROMs (IKDC, Lysholm, and ACL-RSI).
RESULTS: At mid-term follow-up (mean 4.1 ± 1.2 years for repair, 4.2 ± 1.2 years for meniscectomy; p = 0.59), no significant differences existed in strength (quadriceps/hamstring LSI 60°/s and 180°/s), dynamic balance (Y-balance), hop tests (SLH, SLCH, and SLTH), or PROMs (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: At mid-term follow-up (2-5 years), concomitant meniscal repair yielded objective functional performance and patient-reported outcomes equivalent to partial meniscectomy in highly active patients undergoing ACLR, despite more restrictive early rehabilitation. These findings indicate that the initial postoperative restrictions associated with repair do not result in persistent functional deficits. Although meniscal preservation confers established long-term chondroprotective advantages, the present analysis addresses functional parity only; the surgical strategy should weigh both mid-term function and long-term joint health on an individual basis.

title: Minimally Invasive Zadek Osteotomy vs Open Achilles Debridement for Insertional Achilles Tendinopathy in Athletes: A Retrospective Comparative Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common cause of posterior heel pain in athletic populations and may require surgical intervention following failed conservative management. Minimally invasive Zadek osteotomy (MIS Zadek) has emerged as an alternative to traditional open Achilles tendon debridement with Haglund resection, with potential advantages in recovery and complication profile.
METHODS: A retrospective comparative cohort study was performed including 50 athletic patients with IAT (25 MIS Zadek, 25 open surgery) treated between 2022 and 2024 at a single high-volume centre. All patients participated in regular sports activity and failed at least 6 months of nonoperative treatment. The primary outcome was time to return to sport. Secondary outcomes included return-to-sport rate, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) physical function (PF), PROMIS pain interference (PI), and postoperative complications. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to adjust for potential confounders.
RESULTS: Return to sport was achieved in 100% of MIS patients (25/25) and 92% of open patients (23/25; P = .49). Time to return to sport was shorter following MIS Zadek (4.3 ± 1.2 vs 6.1 ± 1.5 months; mean difference -1.8 months, 95% CI -2.6 to -1.0; P < .001). MIS remained independently associated with faster return to sport (adjusted β = -1.6 months, 95% CI -2.4 to -0.8; P < .001). Both groups showed substantial and clinically meaningful improvements in PROMIS outcomes. At 6 months, PROMIS PF was higher in the MIS group (56.5 ± 5.8 vs 52.3 ± 6.4; mean difference +4.2, 95% CI 0.6-7.8; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.69), with a similar pattern for PROMIS PI (47.2 ± 5.5 vs 51.1 ± 6.0; mean difference -3.9, 95% CI -7.1 to -0.7; P = .02; Cohen d = 0.67). By 18 months, PROMIS PF improved further in both groups with comparable outcomes (59.4 ± 4.9 vs 57.8 ± 5.2; mean difference +1.6, 95% CI -1.4 to 4.6; P = .29), and PROMIS PI similarly converged (44.8 ± 4.9 vs 46.3 ± 5.1; mean difference -1.5, 95% CI -4.4 to 1.4; P = .30). Complication rates were lower in the MIS group (2/25, 8%) compared with the open group (6/25, 24%; P = .25), although this difference did not reach statistical significance.
CONCLUSION: MIS Zadek osteotomy was associated with faster return to sport and improved early recovery compared with open surgery; with the numbers available, no significant difference in long-term functional outcomes could be detected. Complications were numerically less frequent following MIS Zadek osteotomy, although this difference did not reach statistical significanceLevel of Evidence:Level III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

title: Can Psychological Readiness Predict Successful Return to Sports After Patellar Stabilization Surgery in Adolescent Patients? A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: While many metrics are used to subjectively assess a patient's knee function with patellofemoral instability (PFI), psychological readiness to return to sport (RTS) after patellar stabilization surgery is not well established in this population. The Anterior Cruciate Ligament Return to Sport After Injury (ACL-RSI) scale assesses psychological readiness to RTS after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and may be similarly beneficial in understanding this domain in those with PFI.
HYPOTHESIS: Higher ACL-RSI scores in patients with PFI are associated with an increased likelihood of RTS after patellar stabilization surgery.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of adolescent patients (10-19 years old) treated surgically for PFI (medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction [MPFLR] with or without tibial tubercle osteotomy) at a single institution from January 2020 to October 2024. Patients actively participating in sports at their first orthopaedic visit who completed the ACL-RSI during postoperative rehabilitation were included. Patient demographics, injury characteristics, surgical procedure, ACL-RSI scores, and RTS status were recorded. Descriptive statistics and bivariate analysis were performed. Based on the euclidean distance, the optimal ACL-RSI cutoff score for predicting successful RTS was determined, and diagnostic accuracy was evaluated with a receiver operating curve. A multivariate logistic regression, adjusted for sex, was used to identify predictors of RTS.
RESULTS: Study criteria identified 97 patients with a median (IQR) age of 15.6 years (14.2-16.4). Seventy underwent isolated MPFLR and 27 underwent MPFLR with tibial tubercle osteotomy. Successful RTS was achieved in 78.3% (n = 76). RTS was associated with higher ACL-RSI scores (P = .012), isolated MPFLR (P = .011), and male sex (P = .03). An ACL-RSI score ≥59.2 was identified as being indicative of successful RTS (area under the curve, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.56-0.83). While procedure type and ACL-RSI scores were both associated with RTS in univariate analysis, the multivariable analysis adjusting for sex revealed that the ACL-RSI cutoff remained the only significant predictor of RTS (odds ratio, 3.56; 95% CI, 1.10-11.51; P = .033).
CONCLUSION: ACL-RSI scores ≥59.2 are associated with an increased likelihood of successful RTS after surgical treatment for PFI in adolescents. Patient demographics and the studied injury characteristics do not appear to influence the likelihood of successful RTS.

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.
