title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction and Mental Health: A Bidirectional Relationship.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: New-onset mental health (MH) conditions are a concern for patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Patients with pre-existing MH conditions have been observed to experience poorer postoperative outcomes.
HYPOTHESIS: Patients with pre-existing MH diagnoses would report poorer outcomes after ACL reconstruction, and non-sport-related injuries would be associated with a greater incidence of new MH diagnoses.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Adults undergoing ACL reconstruction between October 2016 and October 2023 at a large university-affiliated practice were included. Patients completed the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Health and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcomes Score (KOOS) before surgery, and at multiple postoperative timepoints. MH diagnoses included anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, and other psychiatric conditions documented through medications, International Classification of Diseases, tenth revision codes or chart notes. Continuous and categorical variables were compared using appropriate univariate tests, and mixed-model linear regression was used to compare patient-reported outcomes over time while controlling for patient sex.
RESULTS: Out of 365 patients undergoing ACL reconstruction, 50 (13.7%) had a pre-existing MH diagnosis (mean age, 36.42; 84.0% female). Groups did not differ on any scale at baseline except PROMIS Mental Health, which was lower among patients with a pre-existing MH diagnosis (47.3 vs 53.6; P < 0.001). The MH Group reported significantly worse KOOS scores at 2 weeks postoperatively, but no differences were observed thereafter. Among 315 patients without previous history of MH disorder (mean age, 32.90; 52.7% female), 8 (2.5%) developed a new MH diagnosis at 1-year follow-up. Patients aged ≤25 years demonstrated significantly higher baseline KOOS scores than patients >25 years. Among 294 sport-related injuries and 71 non-sport-related injuries, non-sport-related injuries were associated with lower baseline KOOS and PROMIS scores, and higher incidence of new MH diagnoses (7% vs 1.6%; P = 0.02).
CONCLUSION: No differences in KOOS outcomes beyond 2 weeks were found between patients with and without a pre-existing MH condition. Furthermore, non-sport-related injuries were associated with a higher rate of new MH diagnoses.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings may help clinicians identify patients who could benefit from additional support during recovery.

title: Autologous Peripheral Blood-Derived Stem Cells Combined with Platelet-Rich Plasma is Associated With Clinical and Radiological Improvement in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Ruptures-Preliminary Clinical and MRI Findings in 47 Consecutive Patients.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures are common injuries in young and active individuals and can lead to long-term functional impairment and early onset osteoarthritis. While ACL reconstruction remains the standard of care, recent evidence suggests that spontaneous healing may be possible in selected cases. Regenerative and biologic treatment concepts have therefore gained increasing interest. This study investigates the clinical and radiological outcomes of a stem cell-based regenerative treatment for traumatic ACL ruptures and presents findings as preliminary observational evidence.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective case series, 47 patients with isolated partial and complete traumatic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures were treated using a biologic, non-surgical protocol. Diagnosis of an ACL rupture was confirmed by standardized clinical examination (Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot shift test) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which was additionally used to assess rupture morphology and synovial sheath integrity. All patients underwent an ultrasound-guided injection of autologous biologic products derived from peripheral venous blood, consisting of 8 mL of an autologous blood-derived stem cell preparation (BSC), comprising approximately 2-3 mL of concentrated mononuclear cells suspended in 6 mL of autologous platelet-containing plasma, injected directly into the torn ACL. Patients were allowed immediate full weight-bearing without bracing and followed a standardized physiotherapy program. Clinical follow-up was conducted for 12 months, including assessment of pain (VAS), functional outcomes (IKDC, Lysholm), return-to-sport timelines, and MRI-based evaluation of ligament morphology.
RESULTS: The mean age of the cohort was 28.1 years (95% CI 26.0-30.2). Functional outcomes improved continuously throughout follow-up, with mean IKDC and Lysholm scores of 93.6 (95% CI 92.4-94.8) and 94.0 (95% CI 92.7-95.3), respectively, at 12 months. Pain levels decreased markedly, reaching a mean VAS score of 0.36 (95% CI 0.19-0.53). Patients returned to running after a mean of 2.19 weeks (95% CI 1.93-2.45), and most resumed their pre-injury activity level by one year. No infections or re-ruptures occurred and only one secondary ACL reconstruction was recorded. Patients with an intact synovial sheath demonstrated faster return to pivoting sports (26.8 vs. 33.2 weeks) compared with patients with a complete ACL rupture. MRI at 3 months showed evidence of improved ligament morphology in all but one patient.
CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary case series suggests that stem cell-based biologic stimulation may be associated with functional recovery and radiological improvement in selected patients with ACL ruptures. Prospective controlled trials are required to validate these findings.

title: Upper-Extremity Tendinopathy and Enthesopathy in the Athlete: Best Evidence in Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances.
abstract: Tendinopathy and enthesopathy represent common overuse conditions in athletic populations and frequently affect the upper extremity, particularly the rotator cuff, elbow extensor origin, and wrist extensors. These conditions arise predominantly from mechanical overload and are characterized clinically by load-dependent pain and impaired function. Following clinical evaluation, diagnostic evaluation frequently requires multimodality to exclude alternative pathology or inflammatory disease. Exercise-based rehabilitation remains the foundation of management, with contemporary evidence supporting progressive, individualized loading programs, including eccentric, concentric, isometric, and heavy slow resistance protocols, are tailored to symptom severity and sport-specific demands. Adjunctive modalities such as extracorporeal shock wave therapy demonstrate benefit in select chronic cases, particularly lateral epicondylitis and calcific shoulder tendinopathy. Although nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and corticosteroid injections may provide short-term symptom relief, corticosteroids are associated with inferior long-term outcomes and potential deleterious effects on tendon structure. Biologic therapies, including platelet-rich plasma and topical glyceryl trinitrate, demonstrate heterogeneous results, and high-volume image-guided injections remain selectively used in refractory cases. Surgical intervention is reserved for patients with persistent symptoms following 6 to 12 months of comprehensive nonoperative care because most individuals achieve symptom resolution without operative management. Open, arthroscopic, and percutaneous techniques demonstrate comparable outcomes. Emerging technologies, including in-office nanoarthroscopy and bioinductive collagen scaffolds, show early promise but require further high-quality investigation.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: Learned helplessness is associated with jump-landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Persistent biomechanical alterations following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) contribute to reduced functional performance, increased reinjury risk, and diminished joint health. Rehabilitation emphasizes strength and functional restoration; however, neurobehavioral adaptations may persist. Learned helplessness, characterized by reduced motivation, maladaptive biomechanics, and learned non-use of the reconstructed limb, may relate to post-operative neuromuscular control. However, its relationship with dynamic movement after ACLR remains unclear. This study examined the association between learned helplessness and bilateral lower extremity kinematics during jump-landings in individuals following ACLR.
METHODS: Thirty-three individuals with primary, unilateral ACLR completed a learned helplessness scale and jump-landing task with three-dimensional lower-extremity kinematics. Sagittal and frontal plane knee and hip angles were assessed at initial contact and peak landing. Correlations and regression analyses examined associations with learned helplessness, controlling for age, sex, and time since surgery.
FINDINGS: Participants were 2.78 ± 2.78 years post-ACLR and demonstrated low helplessness scores. Greater learned helplessness was moderately associated with greater peak knee abduction in the ACLR limb (r = 0.564, p = 0.001). Weak associations were also observed with reduced peak hip flexion in the ACLR (r = -0.370, p = 0.048) and contralateral limbs (r = -0.415, p = 0.025), which did not survive sensitivity analyses. Learned helplessness was independently associated with greater peak knee abduction angle in the ACLR limb (B = 0.230, p = 0.007). The overall model accounted for 34.8% of the variance in peak knee abduction.
INTERPRETATION: Learned helplessness appears to be associated with frontal plane knee mechanics following ACLR. Consideration of psychological and neurobehavioral constructs in rehabilitation and return-to-sport assessment following ACLR is important.

title: Efficacy of Apparent Diffusion Coefficient Sampling in Muscle Tears and Intersex Differences in Professional Football Players: A Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for monitoring the evolution of muscle injuries in athletes, although no established quantitative measure of recovery currently exists.
HYPOTHESIS: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values may provide a quantitative measure of muscle healing, and sex-related differences may exist in the evolution of muscle injuries.
STUDY DESIGN: Single-center retrospective observational cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2a.
METHODS: Twenty-six professional football (soccer) players (13 male ,13 female) undergoing MRI for muscle injury were retrospectively selected between October 2020 and June 2024. All athletes underwent MRI at baseline (T0) and at 2-week follow-up, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) acquisitions with b values of 0-100-800 s/mm². Two musculoskeletal radiologists measured ADC values within the index lesions at each examination. Changes in ADC between the two time points (ΔADC) were assessed using a paired-samples t test, while sex-related differences were evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test.
RESULTS: The overall mean ADC value at the lesion site decreased from 2.06 ± 0.35 mm2/s at T0 to 1.61 ± 0.30 mm2/s at follow-up corresponding to a mean ΔADC of 0.44 ± 0.20 and a 21.84% reduction. The difference between T0 and follow-up was statistically significant (t = 8.12; P < 0.001). Mean ΔADC values were 0.32 ± 0.20 mm²/s in male players and 0.56 ± 0.25 mm²/s in female players, respectively, with a statistically significant difference between sexes (z = -2.95; P = 0.003). When only hamstring injuries were considered, female players showed a significantly greater decrease in ADC over time than male players (Mann-Whitney U test; exact P = 0.02), with mean ΔADC values of 0.56 ± 0.30 and 0.26 ± 0.08 mm²/s, respectively.
CONCLUSION: Muscle injury is associated with an acute increase in ADC values followed by a progressive decrease during healing. ADC may therefore represent a quantitative imaging biomarker for monitoring muscle recovery.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ADC measurement within muscle tears may provide a quantitative assessment of healing status and support individualized rehabilitation strategies in athletes. Sex-related differences may exist in injury pathophysiology and recovery patterns relevant to safe return to play.

title: Discriminant and Prognostic Validity of the Multimodal Exertional Test (MET) for Athletes with Concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exertional tests have become an informative tool to assist with clinical concussion management and return-to-sport medical decisions. However, current tests are resource intensive and thus, we developed a widely accessible, multimodal exertional test (MET). The objectives of this study were: (1) To evaluate the discriminant validity of the MET by examining sex-stratified differences in symptoms, heart rate (HR), and performance metrics between concussed and healthy athletes; and (2) To assess the predictive (prognostic) validity of the MET by determining whether week 1 MET performance predicts time to medical clearance.
METHODS: This study was conducted at a single academic institution and affiliated sport medicine clinic in Toronto, Canada, with participants recruited between August 2022 and November 2024. 115 interuniversity athletes (female n=49, male n=66) completed the MET at off-season and 55 interuniversity athletes with concussion (female n=37, male n=18) completed the MET up to six times at 1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, 6-, and 8-weeks post-injury. Average and maximum HR, symptoms, performance metrics, and MET pass/fail status were measured prior to and during the protocol. Probabilistic hierarchical models were implemented to estimate differences between concussion and healthy athletes (discriminant validity) and negative binomial analyses were used to examine whether MET performance predicted time to medical clearance (predictive validity).
RESULTS: At 1-week post injury, concussed athletes exhibited greater symptom provocation during the MET compared to healthy athletes, with differences after each task. MET failure rates were highest during weeks 1 (63%) and 2 (49%) and declined through week 8. Athletes who passed the MET at week 1 recovered 20.6 days faster (90% Credible Interval [CrI] = 4.9-36.8 days, posterior probability [pprob] > 0 = 97.7%) than those who failed.
CONCLUSION: The MET demonstrates discriminant validity by eliciting greater symptom provocation in athletes with concussion compared to healthy athletes. Improvements in symptoms and completion rates over 8 weeks indicate recovery-related gains in exertional tolerance. The MET also demonstrates predictive validity, as passing the test at week 1 was associated with faster time to medical clearance, supporting its potential utility as an early prognostic tool in concussion management.

title: Associations of cardiac autonomic modulation and urinary adrenal hormones with marathon finishing time in middle-aged male athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The autonomic nervous and endocrine systems are involved in the physiological adaptation to exercise, and in experimental settings both the sympathovagal balance and the adrenal function are associated with athletic performance. In this real-life field study, the association between non-invasive markers of cardiac autonomic modulation, urinary adrenal hormone levels, and marathon finishing time in middle-aged Caucasian male athletes was investigated.
METHODS: A prospective study was conducted in male marathon runners aged ≥30 years. Continuous single-lead electrocardiographic (ECG) recordings were obtained using a wearable chest device from the day before the marathon until after its completion. Urinary adrenal hormone levels were measured before and after the race. Univariate linear regression analyses were performed to correlate general characteristics, nocturnal heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, and hormonal parameters with marathon finishing time. A multivariable model was then applied including age, body mass index (BMI), and training hours.
RESULTS: 104 athletes were enrolled in the study and 73 (median age 48 years, interquartile range = 16) had adequate data quality for the final analysis. Several HRV parameters correlated with better performance at univariate analysis; lower minimum nocturnal heart rate and vagal predominance, expressed as higher 2 Like Variations (2LV) values remained independently associated with shorter finishing time. Among hormonal variables, the post-/pre-race ratio of urinary normetanephrine hourly output and cortisol/cortisone ratio remained significant at multivariable analysis. Only BMI, but not age and training history, remained significant in a model integrating HRV and hormones.
CONCLUSIONS: Under real-world marathon conditions, specific HRV indices and endocrine markers showed promising value as indicators of physiological readiness with endurance exercise in male master athletes.

title: Neurocognitive Factors in ACL Injury: The Missing Piece in Rehabilitation and Prevention? A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Increasing evidence suggests that ACL injury should not be classified solely as a musculoskeletal condition, but rather as a neurophysiological injury. Several neurocognitive domains, including dual-task interference, visual attention, reaction time and cognitive fatigue, have been proposed as contributors to ACL injury. However, no studies have looked to explore subsections of these neurocognitive domains and their proposed mechanisms into prevention and injury risk. The purpose of this scoping review was to investigate the role of neurocognitive tasks in ACL injury.
STUDY DESIGN: Scoping review.
METHODS: The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR Checklist). Literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus and PEDro databases for studies published between 2006 and 2026. Search terms included combinations of "ACL", "dual-task", "neurocognitive", "reaction time", "visual attention", "decision making", "mental fatigue", "processing speed", and "cognitive interference". Screening was performed by a single reviewer, including publications at all levels of evidence, published in English or Italian.
RESULTS: Forty-two studies were included in the review. Dual-task interference and visual attention were the most investigated neurocognitive domains, with nine studies combining dual-task interference and visual attention and 10 studies combining dual-task interference, visual attention and reaction time. Six studies examined dual-task interference alone, five studies examined visual attention alone, and three studies examined reaction time alone. Cognitive fatigue was examined either alone or combined with other domains in seven studies. Neurocognitive training interventions demonstrated potential benefits in improving visuomotor efficiency, movement compliance and return to sport readiness after ACL rehabilitation. However, current evidence is predominantly derived from laboratory-based and exploratory studies with limited prospective and clinically translational data.
CONCLUSIONS: Neurocognitive factors appear to represent one of the major missing components in current ACL rehabilitation and prevention frameworks. Integrating neurocognitive challenges into rehabilitation and RTS testing may help clinicians better identify athletes at risk for secondary injury. Future research should prioritize prospective, clinically translational studies, as current evidence is predominantly exploratory and laboratory based.

title: Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception tasks in competitive soccer players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional observational study compared jump performance and braking-, propulsion- and landing-phase energetics during self-paced hands-on-hips single-leg countermovement jump (SL-CMJ) and soccer-relevant jump-heading-landing (SR-JHL) between sampled male and female competitive soccer players. A secondary aim examined associations between propulsion-phase knee positive work (generation) and jump height.
METHODS: Forty-five players (22 males, 18.4 ± 2.1 years; 23 females, 20.1 ± 3.5 years) performed SL-CMJ and SR-JHL bilaterally using force plates and three-dimensional motion capture. SR-JHL incorporated a large-screen interactive soccer scene, real-time marker-driven avatar, unrestricted arms, height-scaled virtual-ball heading and tested-limb landing. Limb-averaged outcomes included jump performance, modified reactive strength index (RSI-mod), phase-specific center-of-mass and hip-knee-ankle work and relative joint contribution. Welch tests, Hedges' g and false discovery rate (FDR) correction compared sexes within tasks; mixed-effects models examined knee energetics-jump height associations.
RESULTS: Males had greater jump height and RSI-mod in both tasks (g = 1.34-2.85; q < 0.001), greater propulsion-phase center-of-mass generation and jump center-of-mass net work (g = 0.68-1.35; q ≤ 0.033); however, braking or landing center-of-mass absorption did not differ significantly between groups after FDR correction. Males also showed greater propulsion-phase knee generation, lower ankle generation share, higher knee generation share and greater landing knee absorption. Absolute propulsion-phase knee generation was associated with jump height after accounting for sex and task (β = 0.0147 m per standard deviation; p = 0.042), with a stronger association in SR-JHL (p = 0.006).
CONCLUSION: Differences between the sampled male and female cohorts were concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation, with greater hip and knee work in the male cohort and greater ankle contribution in the female cohort. Propulsion-phase knee positive work was associated with jump height, particularly in SR-JHL. Because sex was inseparable from cohort context, these findings describe between-group differences-not independent sex effects-and provide task-specific comparison context for future anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and return-to-sport research.

title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Athletes: A Narrative Review of Diagnostic Challenges, Management Strategies, and Return-to-Play Outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is a compression disorder involving the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, or subclavian vein within the thoracic outlet. Athletes represent a distinct population in whom delayed diagnosis may result in career-threatening injuries.
OBJECTIVES: This review aimed to: (i) identify diagnostic pitfalls in athletes not captured by conventional provocative tests; (ii) evaluate conservative and operative management by TOS subtype; (iii) synthesize return-to-play (RTP) rates, timelines, and clearance criteria; and (iv) highlight methodological limitations and propose minimum reporting standards for future athlete-specific studies.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception to July 2026 using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for TOS, its subtypes, Paget-Schroetter syndrome, and athletic populations. Reference lists were hand-searched. Studies addressing TOS diagnosis, classification, pathophysiology, management, or RTP in athletes were eligible regardless of design, reflecting limited randomized evidence. Journal legitimacy was screened using the Kscien's list.
RESULTS: nTOS is the predominant form in athletes and usually improves with 4-6 months of rehabilitation, whereas refractory cases may require surgery. vTOS/Paget-Schroetter syndrome requires urgent thrombolysis and early first-rib resection; aTOS is rare but limb-threatening and requires prompt surgery. Mixed presentations occur in up to 23% of surgical cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Outcomes are favorable with subtype-specific diagnosis and objective RTP criteria. However, evidence is limited by retrospective, single-center studies with pooled subtypes, inconsistent RTP definitions, and selective reporting. Prospective, sport-specific studies using standardized outcomes are needed.

title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication.
HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff.
STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies.
RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Study of Transdermal Buprenorphine Patch versus Oral Etoricoxib for Postoperative Pain Management after Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Randomized Comparative Open-label Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is a widely performed procedure for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, providing significant pain relief, improved joint function, and better quality of life. However, it is associated with substantial postoperative pain, which may delay mobilization, impair rehabilitation, prolong hospital stay, and increase the risk of chronic postoperative pain, thus making effective perioperative analgesia crucial for achieving optimal postoperative outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of transdermal buprenorphine patch versus oral etoricoxib for postoperative pain management in patients undergoing TKA, using Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores at rest and during movement for up to 1 week.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This randomized comparative study enrolled 88 patients of American Society of Anesthesiologists grade I/II after ethical approval. The patients were randomly allocated into two groups of 44 patients each. In Group A, patients received oral etoricoxib (90 mg), 1 h before surgery with a sip of water, and in Group B, patients received a transdermal buprenorphine patch (10 µg/h), 12 h before surgery. For statistical analysis, the Chi-square test and Student's t-test were used.
RESULTS: Statistically significant differences were observed in VAS scores (at rest and during movement), with Group B demonstrating significantly lower pain. Furthermore, rescue analgesic requirements and length of hospital stay were reduced significantly in Group B, thus indicating overall superior postoperative pain control.
CONCLUSION: Transdermal buprenorphine patch offers sustained analgesia (reduced VAS scores) with the potential for fewer systemic side effects, reduced need for additional opioid and rescue analgesic requirements, leading to shorter length of hospital stay.

title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class.
RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

title: Different osteoarthritis progression rates within early-stage knee osteoarthritis: a retrospective cohort study using machine learning cluster analysis from the osteoarthritis initiative database.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disease with varying progression rates among patients within the same severity grade. This study aimed to identify clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes among knees with baseline Kellgren and Lawrence (KL) grade 2 osteoarthritis and to compare their 4-year radiographic progression patterns using baseline radiographic features, lifetime exercise patterns, and demographic characteristics.
METHODS: Data of patients with baseline KL grade 2 from the Osteoarthritis Initiative database were retrieved. Unsupervised clustering was performed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) for dimensionality reduction, followed by hierarchical density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (HDBSCAN) to identify distinct subgroups. The proportion of knees progressing to KL grade ≥ 3 within 4 years was compared between subgroups, followed by a survival analysis until knee replacement or progression to KL grade 4.
RESULTS: A total of 1997 knees with a mean follow-up of 103.3 months (maximum, 108 months) were included. A total of seven subgroups were identified and classified into accelerated osteoarthritis progression (AOP) group and slow osteoarthritis progression (SOP) group according to whether their 4-year KL grade progression proportions were above or below the training-set average. In a supportive long-term survival analysis, the AOP group also showed significantly earlier progression to knee replacement or KL grade 4 than the SOP group (training set, P < 0.001; test set, P = 0.049), although the absolute difference in mean survival time was modest (8.3 versus 8.5 years in the training set; 8.4 versus 8.6 years in the test set). The AOP group was characterized mainly by lateral joint space narrowing (JSN) and medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, whereas the SOP group was characterized by medial JSN without subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant patterns without JSN, or chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns; these differences were statistically significant across clusters.
CONCLUSIONS: Within baseline KL grade 2 knees, clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes, including lateral JSN, medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant changes without JSN, and chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns, were associated with different 4-year KL grade progression rates. These findings support viewing KL grade 2 knee OA as a heterogeneous radiographic stage that may be further stratified into phenotype-based subgroups with different short-term radiographic prognoses.

title: Medical resource use by Team USA at the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games: an observational study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To quantify medical resource utilisation among Team USA during the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games, by illness and injury status.
METHODS: This was an epidemiological study of athletes who sought care in the medical clinics in the Athlete Village (n=206). Athletes were categorised as those who incurred injury (INJ; n=77), who incurred physical or mental illness (ILL; n=53) and who had no health concerns (NHC; n=76). The NHC group sought maintenance, recovery and mental performance services. Clinic encounters, encounter time, medical providers and service types accessed (therapy, procedures, pharmacological treatment, diagnostics, advanced imaging) were collected during 26 January-25 February 2026.
RESULTS: 1702 clinical encounters were documented. INJ, ILL and had greater clinic visit numbers per athlete (9.6±7.7, 8.5±8.6 and 7.4±7.2 visits, respectively; p=0.049), with maintenance/massage accounting for most encounters. INJ demonstrated the greatest healthcare needs, with longer clinic time per athlete (5.1±4.2 hours vs 4.3±4.3 hours and 3.8±3.4 hours, respectively; p=0.029), accession of more medical staff provider types, particularly physicians and chiropractors (3.1 provider types vs 2.3 and 1.8 provider types; p<0.001), more procedures and more hospital visits. ILL had the highest use of diagnostic testing and pharmacological interventions (p<0.001). Therapy-based services were used by 87%-100% of all groups. Massage was included in 62%, 66% and 67% of maintenance visits for INJ, ILL and NHC, respectively. Similar proportions of all three groups sought care from athletic trainers (42.0%-58.4%), physical therapists (28.9%-34%), massage therapists (55.3%-66.0%) and psychological service providers (9.2%-24.0%).
CONCLUSION: Medical resource use in this game predominantly involved delivering care to athletes for non-injury/illness reasons. Therefore, it is important to bring healthcare staff with specialised skills in complementary medicine, recovery, mental well-being and performance domains to address needs along the healthcare spectrum.

title: Use of Botanical Ingredients Relevant to Premenstrual Symptoms and Dysmenorrhea Among Elite Female Athletes: Evidence from Doping Control Forms.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and dysmenorrhea can impair training performance in female athletes. Botanical ingredients are commonly used to manage these conditions in the general population, but it is unknown whether elite female athletes do so. This study aimed to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea and determine whether elite female athletes declared them on Doping Control Forms (DCFs).
METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea. Then, DCFs completed during routine anti-doping testing among elite athletes in Poland (2018-2023) were analyzed for declarations of these ingredients, both directly and as components of multi-ingredient products. The proportion of DCFs containing these ingredients was compared between female (n = 4451 DCFs) and male athletes (n = 9068 DCFs; reference) using chi-squared tests.
RESULTS: The review identified 8 and 21 botanical ingredients with evidence for PMS and dysmenorrhea, respectively; of which 9 were detected in DCFs. The most commonly declared ingredients among female athletes were ginger and turmeric/curcuminoid (1.75% and 1.26%, respectively, both studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea). Chasteberry, on the other hand, with the most extensive, albeit low-confidence evidence, for PMS, was rarely declared (0.22%). Direct declaration of ginkgo, valerian, evening primrose oil, and chasteberry was significantly more common among female than male athletes (0.22% vs. 0.02%, 0.36% vs. 0.03%, 0.47% vs. 0.03%, 0.22% vs. 0.02%; adjusted p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Declarations of botanical ingredients studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea were infrequent on DCFs completed by female athletes. Because DCFs do not record the reason for use, these data cannot establish whether declarations reflected treatment of menstrual symptoms; studies assessing indication, symptom status and motivation are needed.

title: Acute Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation Enhances 10-km Outdoor Track Running Performance in Recreational Female Runners.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of acute sodium bicarbonate (SB) supplementation co-ingested with a carbohydrate-rich meal on 10-km running performance and gastrointestinal symptoms in recreational female runners under field-based conditions. Twenty-one healthy women (33.6 ± 4.6 years; body mass index 20.8 ± 1.3 kg/m; maximal oxygen uptake 48.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg-1·min-1) completed two 10-km outdoor track running time trials (TTs) in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Participants ingested either SB (0.3 g/kg body mass [BM]) or placebo (PLA; 0.03 g/kg BM table salt), together with a standardized carbohydrate-rich meal (1.5 g/kg BM), 90 min before exercise during the same phase of the menstrual cycle. Blood pH, bicarbonate [HCO3-], and [lactate] were measured before, and 1, 3, 5, and 7 min after the TTs; performance time was recorded. Gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded at 30, 60, and 90 min after SB and PLA ingestions. Blood pH (7.47 ± 0.03 vs. 7.42 ± 0.04, p < .001) and [HCO3-] (27.7 ± 1.4 vs. 22.2 ± 1.5 mmol/L, p < .001) were higher at rest and remained elevated postexercise following SB compared with PLA (p < .05 for all time points). TT completion time improved after SB compared with PLA (3,046.1 ± 208.7 s vs. 3,078.4 ± 206.8 s; p = .011). No significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms scores were observed between conditions (p > .05 for all). In conclusion, acute co-ingestion of 0.3 g/kg of SB with a carbohydrate-rich meal is a practical and well-tolerated strategy to achieve higher resting blood [HCO3-] and pH as well as to improve 10-km TT running performance in recreational female runners.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Concussion Diagnosis, Management, and Functional Recovery: An Interdisciplinary and Evidence-Based Approach.
abstract: Sport-related concussion is a common and clinically complex form of mild traumatic brain injury with significant academic, occupational, and psychosocial consequences. Management has shifted away from prolonged strict rest to early, symptom-limited activity and targeted rehabilitation. Concussion remains a clinical diagnosis, and routine neuroimaging is typically normal. Symptoms may evolve over hours to days, and structured tools support early assessment; however, they should not be used in isolation to determine recovery or clearance. Office-based evaluation facilitates comprehensive assessment of symptom domains, comorbidities, and functional impact, and subsymptom threshold aerobic exercise testing provides a guide for early activity and individualized progression. Management includes therapies targeted to specific symptom patterns and interdisciplinary care for persistent symptoms. Pharmacologic therapy is symptom targeted and supportive, with limited evidence for select interventions and recommended avoidance of sedating agents that can confound monitoring. Nutritional and dietary supplements have theoretical benefit but insufficient clinical evidence for routine use. Functional recovery is addressed through individualized plans for return to learn, return to play, and return to drive. Prevention should focus on evidence-based risk reduction, with strongest support for policy and rule changes, and equipment and training interventions provide variable benefit. Emerging technologies are primarily research tools given limited standardization and uncertain clinical thresholds.

title: Editorial Commentary: Allograft Reconstruction in Chronic Proximal Hamstring Tendon Avulsions: Bridging the Gap May Not Equal a Full Return.
abstract: Proximal hamstring tendon avulsions are being treated surgically at rising rates, and although primary repair reliably restores function and return to sport in the acute setting, chronic and significantly retracted tears present a far more difficult problem. When direct repair is not feasible for a chronic, retracted proximal hamstring tendon avulsion, allograft reconstruction offers a bridge across a gap that would otherwise go unaddressed. However, significant chronicity and retraction are difficult challenges to overcome, and patient expectations must be appropriately counseled. As a salvage procedure, allograft reconstruction may improve patient outcomes significantly; however, it is not expected to restore full function, return athletic individuals to their baseline and preinjury level of sports participation, or match the success of primary repair. Allograft reconstruction may also carry more than double the risk of rerupture, which is important to discuss with patients up front. Graft choice and postoperative rehabilitation protocols remain heterogeneous across the limited available literature, and a validated tool to risk-stratify which chronic, retracted tears are best served by reconstruction versus continued nonoperative management does not yet exist. These findings suggest that allograft reconstruction is a viable and clinically meaningful option for a difficult, often nonoperatively unsalvageable problem, but surgeons should frame it for patients as a salvage procedure rather than a full restoration of function, and expectations should be set accordingly.

title: Adolescent Sports-Related Lower Extremity Pain and Overuse Injuries.
abstract: Adolescent participation in organized sports has increased substantially in recent decades, accompanied by a rising incidence of lower extremity pain and overuse injuries. Unique physiologic characteristics of the growing athlete, including open physes and periods of rapid skeletal maturation, combined with early sport specialization and increasing training demands, place adolescents at elevated risk for overuse conditions. This review examines common causes of sports-related lower extremity pain in adolescent athletes, including patellofemoral pain syndrome, Osgood-Schlatter disease, patellar tendinopathy, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease, bone stress injuries, and symptomatic flexible flatfoot. For each condition, we review epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic considerations, and contemporary management strategies. Most overuse injuries in this population are diagnosed clinically and respond well to conservative treatment that emphasizes activity modification, progressive rehabilitation, and load management. Imaging should be used judiciously, primarily to confirm diagnosis or exclude alternative pathology. Emerging therapies, including biologic injections and bone stimulation modalities, show promise in select conditions but require further high-quality evidence before routine adoption. Prevention remains central to reducing injury burden. Gradual progression of training load, neuromuscular conditioning, nutritional optimization, and monitoring during growth spurts are key strategies. Increasing evidence also suggests that psychosocial factors may influence injury risk. A multidisciplinary approach involving clinicians, coaches, and strength and conditioning professionals is essential to promote safe, sustainable sports participation and long-term musculoskeletal health in adolescent athletes.

title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. Although most cases resolve with time, accurate diagnosis is essential to distinguish common musculoskeletal causes from more serious conditions. This article reviews key causes of athletic back pain, including muscle strain, mechanical low back pain, spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, lumbar disc herniation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

title: Association Between Early Postoperative Limb Symmetry Index Scores and 2-Year Patient-Reported Outcomes After Quadriceps Tendon Autograft ACL Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The limb symmetry index (LSI) is a measure comparing strength and functional movement between the surgical and nonsurgical limbs, used after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) to guide rehabilitation and assess return-to-sport readiness. With increasing use of the quadriceps tendon autograft (QT-ACLR), limited data exist on whether the LSI score correlates with patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: To evaluate the predictive value of postoperative strength and functional LSI tests at 3, 6, and 9 months for short-term PROMs, determine Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) thresholds, and assess differences based on PASS achievement. It was hypothesized that quadriceps strength LSI score would more strongly predict 2-year PROMs than hamstring strength LSI score, and that higher 9-month isokinetic quadriceps LSI scores would be associated with higher International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) and Lysholm scores.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: Patients undergoing primary QT-ACLR from 2021 to 2024 with LSI testing during rehabilitation (isometric and isokinetic lower extremity strength, Y-Balance, hop testing) and no revision or additional knee surgery were included. The LSI score was assessed at 3, 6, and 9 months, and PROMs, including Lysholm and IKDC scores, were collected at a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years. Multivariable linear regression was used to evaluate associations between LSI measures and PROMs after adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to determine PASS thresholds.
RESULTS: A total of 100 knees in 100 patients (mean age, 25.3 ± 11.2 years; BMI, 25.9 ± 6.5 kg/m2; 52% male) were included. Quadriceps and hamstring strength and functional performance progressively improved from 3 to 9 months, with the LSI score reaching 77% to 81% for quadriceps strength and 98% to 100% for hamstring strength by 9 months postoperatively. At a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years, the mean satisfaction score was 8.4 of 10, the Lysholm score was 90.7, and the IKDC score was 77.8. Linear regression, adjusted for age, sex, and BMI, demonstrated that 3-month isometric quadriceps LSI score had a strong effect on IKDC score, explaining substantial variance (β = 3.9; adjusted R2 [AdjR2] = 0.36; P < .03); 6-month isokinetic quadriceps and hamstrings showed moderate but significant effects (β = 2.9-3.7; AdjR2 = 0.13-0.17; P < .05) on IKDC score; and 9-month fast quadriceps had a strong effect explaining substantial variance in Lysholm and IKDC scores (β = 3.9-4.7; AdjR2 = 0.34-0.35; P ≤ .003). Lysholm and IKDC scores correlated with satisfaction and accurately discriminated PASS thresholds (area under the curve, 0.927-0.937; P < .001). Patients achieving the IKDC PASS demonstrated higher LSI scores across time points and all PROMs.
CONCLUSION: After QT-ACLR, strength-associated LSIs were independently associated with PROMs at a mean 2-year follow-up, after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI. Early isometric quadriceps strength at 3 months predicted higher 2-year IKDC scores, with PASS achievers generally attaining a 60% to 70% LSI score by 3 months. Isokinetic quadriceps strength at 9 months predicted both IKDC and Lysholm scores. These findings highlight the importance of early quadriceps strength recovery and the value of LSI measures in predicting PROMs and informing early rehabilitation.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Tendon Dry Needling for Recalcitrant Distal Biceps Tendinopathy: A Case Series.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Distal biceps brachii insertional tendinopathy occurs in approximately 2.6 per 100,000 individuals per year, more commonly affecting middle-aged males. Dry needling with percutaneous tendon fenestration is a common treatment for insertional tendinopathies. However, little evidence supports this treatment for the distal biceps tendon, likely secondary to difficult access without ultrasound guidance. This case series describes the treatment of two subjects with chronic distal biceps tendinopathy using ultrasound-guided percutaneous tendon dry needling with fenestration and a graded loading program in outpatient physical therapy.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series.
METHODS: Two recreationally active adults with chronic distal biceps tendon pathology underwent clinical and sonographic examination, with images reviewed by clinicians registered in musculoskeletal sonography (RMSK). Subject A (55 years of age) presented with a partial distal biceps tendon tear, and Subject B (46 years of age) presented with distal biceps tendinosis. Both had pain and exercise-related functional limitations, and each participated in a physical therapy plan of care consisting of one visit per week for five weeks, including ultrasound-guided tendon dry needling for the first three weeks and graded isotonic loading of the distal biceps tendon throughout. Each subject transitioned to a guided home exercise program and was reassessed 3 and 6 months from the evaluation date. Subject-reported outcome measures included the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS), the Upper Extremity Functional Index (UEFI-20), and the Global Rating of Change (GROC) at baseline, 5 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months.
RESULTS: At five weeks, both subjects exceeded the minimal clinically important difference for each outcome measure. These results persisted at six months, with notable tendon healing characteristics visualized with diagnostic ultrasound.
CONCLUSIONS: Percutaneous ultrasound-guided tendon dry needling with fenestration as an adjunct to a graded tendon loading program may have contributed to reduced pain and disability among two individuals with distal biceps tendinopathy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury induces neuroplastic changes within the central nervous system (CNS) that may persist beyond reconstruction and rehabilitation.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose was to compare neurocognitive performance and cortical oscillatory activity between open-skill athletes (eg, soccer, basketball, or handball players) without ACL injury history and athletes with ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during a probabilistic go/no-go task. It was hypothesized that athletes with ACLR would exhibit poorer behavioral performance and less efficient oscillatory dynamics, particularly higher theta and lower suppression of beta and alpha power oscillations after goal stimulus onset.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 90 open-skill athletes (45 non-ACLR, 45 ACLR) performed a probabilistic go/no-go task while electroencephalographic recording was performed. Time-frequency analysis targeted midfrontal theta (4-7 Hz), left-lateralized central beta (15-25 Hz), and posterior alpha (8-12 Hz) oscillations during prestimulus and target stimulus windows. Linear mixed-effects models examined group differences in cognitive performance and oscillatory power.
RESULTS: Athletes with ACLR showed slower response times and lower accuracy (d = 0.75-1.09). Midfrontal theta power was attenuated for the ACLR group during the prestimulus phase (d = 0.60) yet elevated during target phase trials (d = 0.48), indicating a shift from proactive to reactive cognitive control in athletes with ACLR. Left-lateralized central beta (d = 0.61) and posterior alpha suppression (d = 0.55) were reduced, reflecting impaired motor cortical disinhibition and less efficient visual-attentional resource deployment, especially under high uncertainty conditions.
CONCLUSION: Athletes with ACLR showed persistent alterations in the cortical oscillatory mechanisms associated with conflict monitoring, motor preparation, and attentional allocation under uncertainty. These neurocognitive alterations may compromise adaptive motor responses in sport contexts characterized by high uncertainty and cognitive mental demand, potentially increasing reinjury risk. These findings support the integration of neurocognitive assessment into return-to-sport protocols.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Alterations in cortical oscillatory dynamics during decision-making under uncertainty may reflect reduced efficiency in cognitive control, motor preparation, and attentional allocation, which are not detected by standard assessments. Exercise professionals should consider integrating these assessments into return-to-sport protocols to address the persistent CNS alterations that may underlie reinjury risk in athletes with ACLR.

title: Conductive Composite-Based Wearable Sensors for Sports Science: Intelligent Data Analysis and Emerging Applications.
abstract: Wearable sensors enable continuous acquisition of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals during exercise, providing data to support sports performance assessment, training regulation, fatigue monitoring, and rehabilitation interventions. However, signal reliability and multidimensional data analysis under complex motion conditions remain constrained by device functionality. Conductive composites can improve sensor flexibility, interfacial conformability, and signal acquisition performance, while artificial intelligence (AI) enables movement pattern recognition, state assessment, and outcome prediction from complex data. Their integration is advancing wearable systems toward multimodal sensing and intelligent analysis. Guided by application needs in sports, this review summarizes emerging applications of wearable sensing technologies enabled by conductive composites and AI. First, the relevance to sports science and the data characteristics of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals are introduced. The functional characteristics, representative applications, and major limitations of conductive polymer, carbon-based, MXene, and hydrogel composites are then summarized. Regarding algorithms, the fundamental principles of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) are discussed, with comparisons of their capabilities in feature extraction, temporal modeling, and multisource data analysis, as well as their input data requirements. On this basis, advances in the application of these systems to sports performance and sport-specific movement monitoring, exercise-induced fatigue monitoring and assessment, sports injury identification and evaluation, and intelligent monitoring of sports rehabilitation are reviewed followed by a discussion of current challenges and future directions. Through the coordinated integration of material design, signal acquisition, and intelligent analysis, wearable systems are expected to enable continuous, reliable, and individualized assessment of exercise-related states, with further applications in real-time feedback, risk alerts, and training decision support, providing a technological foundation for scientifically informed training, sports rehabilitation, and individual health management.

title: Repeated sprint training in hypoxia as a post-surgical rehabilitation strategy: A case study in an elite badminton player.
abstract: Badminton is a racquet sport that imposes high demands on both aerobic and anaerobic capacity and involves repetitive, high-intensity movements, increasing the risk of non-contact injuries to joints and muscle-tendon units. Returning to sport-specific conditioning after injury, particularly post-surgery, presents challenges for deconditioned athletes seeking to restore aerobic capacity while minimising mechanical stress imposed on the injured parts. This case study evaluated the feasibility of integrating short-term repeated sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) as a supplementary modality within a late-stage post-lower back surgery rehabilitation program to support aerobic reconditioning before return to sport-specific conditioning. An elite men's singles badminton athlete completed 4-week RSH (FiO2 ~ 16.5%), alongside his regular rehabilitation schedule. The intervention consisted of 20 × 4-s all-out cycling sprints interspersed with 30-56-s recovery, performed once weekly. Post-intervention lactate profiling suggested a rightward shift in the blood lactate curve, with estimated increases of 33% and 10% in power output at the aerobic and anaerobic thresholds, respectively, indicative of aerobic reconditioning. However, the present findings should be interpreted cautiously due to observed stage-to-stage blood lactate variability, single-case design, and concurrent rehabilitation. Overall, the present study supports the feasibility of incorporating hypoxic RSH in late-stage rehabilitation to facilitate return to sport-specific conditioning.

title: Low energy availability, disordered eating, exercise dependence, and injury prevalence in female CrossFit® athletes.
abstract: CrossFit® incorporates high-intensity, multimodal training with strong elements of community and competition. Despite known physical and psychological benefits, musculoskeletal injury prevalence ranges from 15 to 75%. Due to training demands, CrossFit® athletes may be at risk for low energy availability (LEA), disordered eating (DE), and exercise dependence (EXD), which may increase injury risk. Female CrossFit® participants (n = 198) completed an online survey including the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), Exercise Dependence Scale (EDS-21), and Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q). Participants were classified as DE only, primary EXD, secondary EXD (DE + EXD), or control (no DE or EXD risk). Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Overall, 37.8% of participants were at risk for LEA, 43.9% for DE, and 15.1% for EXD. Participants with secondary EXD had significantly (p < 0.001) higher EDE-Q global scores (3.9 ± 1.0) compared to primary EXD (1.4 ± 0.7) and control groups (1.0 ± 0.7). Additionally, 71.7% reported exercising despite injury, and 45.4% reported an injury within the past year. The prevalence of LEA, DE, and EXD was comparable to prior research; however, the high proportion of athletes continuing to train while injured suggests EXD-related behaviors may contribute to injury prevalence among CrossFit® athletes. These findings underscore the importance of early screening and education on adequate fueling and healthy training behaviors to support long-term health, performance, and injury prevention.

title: How Effectively Does Protective Sports Gear Prevent Sports Injuries?
abstract: As organized and recreational sports continue to grow in popularity, associated sports injuries increasingly burden athletes. Protective sports gear is intended to reduce injury risk during play. This article provides a comprehensive review of the mechanism and efficacy of protective sports gear in injury prevention to the head and neck, upper extremity, and lower extremity and assesses where perhaps evidence for protection is lacking. Helmets, face shields, and protective eyewear have clear benefits in structural protection against injury. The impact of sports gear in reducing sport-related concussion is more variable, largely due to the repetitive nature of the injury mechanism where cumulative low-magnitude impacts contribute to brain injury. For the upper extremity, wrist guards have a clear benefit in reducing major and minor injuries among gymnasts and snowboarders and hence by inference on other impact sports. Ankle braces and taping potentially reduce the risk of ankle sprains among athletes, and the mandating of shin guards in professional soccer results in decreased sports-related lower extremity fractures. Further research is warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of sports gear on reinjury prevention and to study the implications of sports gear on risk compensation theory in athletes.

title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
abstract: Akbaş, A, Hadyk, V, Bryk, P, Mazzei, S, Stanula, A, and Juras, G. Large-scale evaluation of performance and biological maturation in post-PHV youth soccer players: Sprinting, jumping, aerobic fitness, and functional movement. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to provide an integrated developmental profile of adolescent soccer players by examining how chronological age, biological maturation, and functional movement quality interact to shape sprint, jump, and aerobic fitness performance. A total of 246 male athletes (U15-U17) from 5 elite youth soccer academies completed sprint, jump, change-of-direction (COD), and aerobic tests alongside Functional Movement Screen (FMS) and Y-Balance Test (YBT) assessments. Maturity offset (years from peak height velocity, PHV) was used to estimate biological age, and group differences were analyzed using analysis of variance and analysis of covariance, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements with age were observed in sprinting, jumping, and aerobic fitness (p < 0.001); however, after controlling for PHV, differences in jumping and COD performance were no longer significant, whereas sprint performance and aerobic fitness remained age-dependent. Functional movement and balance showed small age-related differences that were largely explained by maturational variation. Weak and inconsistent correlations between FMS, YBT, and performance (|r| ≈ 0.20-0.35) suggested partial independence between movement quality and motor output. Notably, in older players, higher scores in mobility-related FMS components were associated with slower sprinting, a pattern that may reflect-rather than cause-reduced mechanical efficiency associated with greater flexibility. These findings indicate that post-PHV players are not a homogeneous group and support the use of maturity-informed, multidimensional athlete monitoring to guide individualized training even after PHV.

title: Comparison of Achilles tendon loading between rocker-soled and advanced footwear technology shoes during running in healthy individuals.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Achilles tendinopathy is a common running-related injury, and footwear characteristics may influence Achilles tendon loading. This study investigated the effects of rocker shoes and advanced footwear technology (AFT) shoes on Achilles tendon (AT) force during running.
METHODS: Nineteen healthy adult males with normal foot posture performed rearfoot strike running at a controlled speed under three footwear conditions: neutral, rocker, and AFT shoes. Peak AT force, AT force impulse per step, ankle joint angle, anterior ground reaction force, and stance time were compared among the three conditions.
RESULTS: No significant differences in ankle joint angle or stance time were observed among the footwear conditions. Compared with neutral and AFT shoes, rocker shoes significantly reduced peak AT force, AT force impulse per step, and peak anterior ground reaction force. No significant differences were observed between AFT and neutral shoes for any AT force-related variable.
CONCLUSIONS: Rocker shoes reduced Achilles tendon loading during running, whereas AFT shoes did not significantly alter Achilles tendon loading compared with neutral shoes. The reduction in tendon loading was accompanied by a lower peak anterior ground reaction force, which may reflect reduced propulsive demand at the ankle joint. Rocker shoes may therefore be beneficial for reducing mechanical loading of the Achilles tendon during running.

title: Foot and Ankle Sports Injuries: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Contemporary Orthopedic Innovations for the General Practitioner.
abstract: General practitioners (GPs) are frequently the first clinicians to evaluate athletic and nonathletic foot and ankle injuries. Six common foot and ankle conditions seen by GPs are Achilles tendon injuries, lateral ankle ligament sprains, plantar plate injuries/turf toe, ankle fractures and syndesmotic injuries, Lisfranc injuries, and fifth metatarsal base fractures. For each condition, this review outlines clinical diagnostic features, appropriate use of imaging, and decision making regarding conservative management strategies versus surgery. Nonoperative management initiated by GPs include functional bracing, protected weight bearing, activity modification, and structured rehabilitation protocols. Indications for orthopedic referral, such as failure of conservative management, mechanical instability or joint laxity on examination, radiographic evidence of displacement or unstable fracture, high-grade ligamentous or plantar plate disruption, and involvement of high-demand athletes, also are reviewed. By understanding common patient presentations, appropriate initial management, and indications for referral to orthopedic specialists, GPs can optimize early care, reduce diagnostic delay, and improve long-term functional outcomes for patients with foot and ankle sports injuries.

title: Gamified Versus Traditional Balance Training: Effects on Balance and Motivation in Collegiate Student-Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gamified balance platforms offer engaging alternatives to traditional balance tools; however, their comparative effectiveness in improving dynamic balance and motivation in athletic populations remains unclear.Hypothesis/Purpose: To compare the effects of gamified (Wii Fit) versus traditional (wobble board) balance training on dynamic balance and intrinsic motivation in collegiate athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Quasi-experimental controlled trial.
METHODS: Thirty healthy collegiate athletes (5 males, 25 females; 19.8 ± 0.9 years) were pseudo-randomized to gamified training (n = 9), traditional training (n = 11), or a control group (n = 10). Participants in the training groups completed twelve 15-minute supervised sessions (three times per week for four weeks). Dynamic balance was assessed pre- and post-intervention using the modified Star Excursion Balance Test (mSEBT) and the Dynamic Postural Stability Index (DPSI). Motivation was evaluated post-training using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI). Group x time differences were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests, and IMI scores were compared between training groups using one-way ANOVAs.
RESULTS: Both training groups showed significant improvements in anterior reach (gamified: +6.5 ± 10.2 cm; traditional: +6.5 ± 10.3 cm) and mSEBT composite scores (gamified: +21.6 ± 11.9 cm, d = 1.84; traditional: +18.5 ± 14.6 cm, d = 1.54) compared with control (-2.3 ± 10.5 cm; p < 0.01). DPSI scores did not change significantly (p > 0.28). IMI interest/enjoyment scores were higher in the gamified group (5.0 ± 1.2) than the traditional group (3.2 ± 1.3; p < 0.01, d = 1.50).
CONCLUSION: Gamified balance training produced similar biomechanical improvements to traditional balance training while eliciting greater enjoyment. It may serve as an engaging option for balance rehabilitation and injury-prevention programs in athletes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 2.
